ABSTRACT

Kelp forests, which are dense stands of brown seaweeds of

the taxonomic order Laminariales, often are used as indica-

tor species for assessing the environmental state of coastal

waters. To this end, large scale monitoring approaches are

required apart from traditional labor-intensive point sampling

techniques. Bio-optical modelling with hyperspectral remote

sensing data provides the possibility to take on the task. Yet,

hyperspectral imagery mainly originates from airborne data.

Within in the scope of the EnMAP Preparatory Program the

bio-optical model WASI-2D was tested to the coastal area of

Helgoland. A simulated EnMAP scene was spectrally un-

mixed for the two substrate types Laminariales and sediment.

Inverse modelling yielded plausible patterns and gradients of

substrate coverages and bathymetry. Comparisons with in situ

data revealed results tended to overestimate sediment and to

underestimate Laminariales coverage and bathymetry. WASI-

2D, however, was able to resolve the complex bottom and

bathymetric structure at the rocky coast of Helgoland.

Index Terms—WASI, hyperspectral, kelp, unmixing,

shallow water

Abstract: HICO, Hyperion and MERIS have already demonstrated the capabilities of hyperspectral sensors to gather information on optical properties in inland waters. With the advent of Sentinel-2, Sentinel-3, EnMap, PRISMA and HyspIRI we expect that application of remote sensing techniques for inland water quality assessment will progress even more. Some clear advantages rely on: 1) improved spatial resolution (so that even medium/small lakes are imaged), 2) increased frequency of overpasses (so that environmental processes are detected in time) and 3) enhanced sensor characteristics (which allow, for instance, the secondary phytoplankton pigments to be retrieved). Water constituents, such as phytoplankton, total suspended matter or coloured dissolved organic matter (CDOM) and, in shallow water, benthic substrate composition are important indicators of lake water quality. Recent monitoring techniques still focus on in-situ sampling at specific measurement points or mapping of benthic substrate composition along diving transects leading to temporal intervals ranging from months to several years. Rapidly changing lake conditions such as bloom events, however, require alternative monitoring approaches, which are able to capture the spatial and temporal dimensions of these changes. Remote sensing is an ideal solution for this purpose. Until recently, the absence of high spatial resolution sensors suitable for inland water body analyses narrowed water remote sensing to large water bodies. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In literature [31], Zhang et al. have also insisted that the l_{2}-norm collaboration may be superior to the l_{1}-norm sparsity in many practical applications, because the collaboration investigates the correlations among classes in representing the query samples. Therefore, in the l_{2}-norm constraint, the correlations among different bands contained in a 3-D spectral data can be well described, which has the potential to improve the fusion performance. However, it should be noted that the l_{2}-norm tends to reduce sparsity, which may decrease the fusion accuracy. Based on these arguments, we find that seeking a tradeoff between the l_{1}-norm and l_{2}-norm constraints to combine the sparsity and collaboration of data can further improve the quality of fusion.

In this study, we design a fusion method based on joint sparse-collaborative representation (SCR) for LS-HSIs and HS-MSIs. Specifically, the sparse and collaborative dictionaries are firstly learned to obtain spectral information from the given LS-HSI. With this model, the corresponding sparse and collaborative coefficients are acquired. Since the sparse coefficient includes strong sparsity accompanied by some collaboration reflecting the correlations among spectral bands, it is employed to reconstruct the HS-HSI by multiplying with the learned sparse spectral dictionary.

The major contributions and novelties of this paper are four-fold. First, we learn the sparse and collaborative dictionaries to describe the spectral information of the given LS-HSI from two perspectives. In particular, a learning model is built to obtain the collaborative spectral dictionary, which focuses on the data collaboration. Second, the turbopixel based segmentation, to the best of our knowledge, is for the first time introduced to solve the fusion problem of LS-HSIs and HS-MSIs, which obtains numerous 3-D patches with unfixed sizes to well reflect complex local structure of the spectral data. Third, the sparse-collaborative representation model is established to determine a tradeoff between sparsity and collaboration and thus achieves much well fusion performance. Forth, the performance of our proposed SCR method is evaluated on three datasets, including the Indian Pines [15], Salinas [34], and Pavia [35] datasets. Experimental results have demonstrated that our method achieves much superiority in the fusion of both LS-HSIs and HS-MSIs, compared with several state-of-the-art methods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we briefly show the preliminaries and motivations of our work. The proposed method for the fusion of LS-HSIs and HS-MSIs is introduced in Section 3. In Section 4, experimental results on three datasets and related discussion are presented. We finally conclude this paper in Section 5.
